jsonld.name: Gammon Steak with Fried Eggs
jsonld.description: The café's king-size plate: a thick, cured gammon steak seared to a mahogany crust, crowned with fried eggs whose yolks run into the meat's scoring, and — the classic trinity completed — grilled tomato or pineapple alongside. Gammon is the breakfast meat that behaves like a steak: dense, salty-sweet from the cure, and almost impossible to ruin, which makes it the most confident plate on any fry-up menu. The technique is simpler than its reputation: a hot pan, a short sear each side, and the small professional touches — scoring the fat rind so it crisps instead of buckling, and resting the steak while the eggs fry in the rendered ham fat. That fat is this recipe's dividend: gammon renders sweet, smoky, deeply savoury fat, and the eggs fried in it are the reason the pairing has held for a century.

skeleton:
Gammon Steak with Fried Eggs

British · Easy · Serves 2

Jump to Recipe Method Troubleshooting Storage
The café's king-size plate: a thick, cured gammon steak seared to a mahogany crust, crowned with fried eggs whose yolks run into the meat's scoring, and — the classic trinity completed — grilled tomato or pineapple alongside. Gammon is the breakfast meat that behaves like a steak: dense, salty-sweet from the cure, and almost impossible to ruin, which makes it the most confident plate on any fry-up menu. The technique is simpler than its reputation: a hot pan, a short sear each side, and the small professional touches — scoring the fat rind so it crisps instead of buckling, and resting the steak while the eggs fry in the rendered ham fat. That fat is this recipe's dividend: gammon renders sweet, smoky, deeply savoury fat, and the eggs fried in it are the reason the pairing has held for a century.

Quantities live in the recipe card.

The gammon

The eggs and plate

To serve

- **Score the fat rind in a crosshatch** — cuts about 5 mm apart through the fat to the flesh line. Untreated rind buckles and curls, lifting the steak off the pan; scored rind crisps flat and bastes the meat as it melts. - **Room temperature and dry:** 15 minutes out of the fridge, patted dry on both faces. Wet gammon steams grey; dry gammon sears mahogany. - **Check for the salt level:** most modern gammon is mild-cured and needs nothing; old-fashioned or home-cured may be aggressive — a quick rinse and thorough dry fixes the fierce ones. - Grill or pan for the pineapple or tomato, heated alongside.

Doneness & Quality Checkpoints

  • Gammon: scored rind crisped flat; 4-minute mahogany sears; probe 65–68 °C.
  • Glaze (if using): lacquered in 60 seconds, never blackened.
  • Eggs: basted in the gammon's rendered fat, lace edges, running yolks.
  • Rest: 3 minutes; the plate assembles during the eggs, not after.

Gammon Steak with Fried Eggs

Prep: 5 minutes · Cook: 15 minutes · Total: 20 minutes · Serves 2

Ingredients

The gammon

  • 2 gammon steaks (about 250 g each), about 1.5–2 cm thick
  • 5 ml / 5 g neutral oil (gammon renders plenty of its own)
  • Optional glaze: 15 g honey and 5 g wholegrain mustard, mixed

The eggs and plate

  • 4 large eggs (220 g)
  • 15 g butter, only if the gammon's fat runs short
  • 2 pineapple rings (100 g) or 2 large tomato halves (250 g), for the grill
  • 2 g black pepper

To serve

  • Fried bread or chips (about 200 g), peas (100 g), or the full English's supporting cast
  • Brown breakfast sauce; tomato ketchup for the chips

Instructions

  1. **Sear the gammon, 4 minutes a side.** Heat the oil in a heavy pan over medium-high until shimmering. Lay in the steaks and sear undisturbed 4 minutes — the underside will go deep mahogany and the fat's crosshatch will begin to crisp and render. Turn and sear 3–4 minutes more. Checkpoint — both faces are deeply browned with dark caramelised edges, the scored fat is golden and crisping at its cuts, and an instant-read probe into the thickest point reads 65–68 °C — cured meat is fully safe at lower temperatures than fresh pork, and this range keeps it juicy. Past 75 °C it tightens and dries; pull at the probe's first reading in range.
  2. **The optional glaze, 60 seconds.** If glazing, brush the honey-mustard over the top face of each steak and flip once more for 30 seconds a side — the sugars catch quickly and turn the crust lacquered and glossy. Checkpoint — the glaze has darkened to a shine without blackening — honey burns in seconds, so this is a brush-flip-flip-and-out move, never a simmer.
  3. **Rest the steak; eggs in the ham fat.** Move the steaks to warm plates to rest — 3 minutes, during which the meat's juices redistribute and the eggs cook. Tilt the pan and check the rendered fat: you want 2–3 mm. Crack in the eggs and fry-baste 2–3 minutes to the butter-basted master's spec — set whites, lace edges, liquid yolks — adding the butter only if the ham's fat runs short. Checkpoint — the eggs fry in sweet-smoky gammon fat, whites fully set with gold fringes, yolks running. The rested steak, pressed gently, shows no flood of juice — it has kept its moisture inside.
  4. **The classic landing.** Steak on the plate, eggs crowning it, grilled pineapple ring or tomato half alongside, pepper over the eggs. Fried bread or chips and peas to complete the café plate, sauces at the ready. Checkpoint — the eating test: the first cut through the steak meets a juicy, springy cure-sweet interior under that mahogany crust; the yolk breaks and runs into the scoring; the pineapple's sharp-sweet bite resets between forkfuls. The plate is enormous and entirely coherent.

Finish & Plate

The café serves this as its "gammon, egg and chips" — steak, eggs, a mound of chips, peas, and both sauces — and that presentation needs no apology. As part of the full-English family, swap the chips for fried bread and the plate joins the canon. Either way: tea, and the quiet satisfaction of a plate that cooks itself in twenty minutes.

Troubleshooting

SymptomCauseFix
Steak curled and buckledRind unscored, or pan too coolThe crosshatch score; a properly shimmering pan
Grey, steaming steakWet surface or crowded panPat dry; one steak at a time if the pan is small
Tough, dry meatOvercooked past 75 °CThe probe at 65–68 °C; cured meat forgives low, not high
Glaze burnt blackSimmered rather than flashedBrush-and-flip only, 30 seconds a side, pan off between
Eggs greasyFat deeper than 3 mmPour the surplus into the chip pan's destiny before the eggs

Storage, Make-Ahead & Variations

- **Cooked gammon keeps 3 days refrigerated** and is the best leftover in the fry-up family: sliced cold into sandwiches, diced into the full-English hash, or flaked into kedgeree. The eggs never hold; the steak improves overnight. - **Variation — gammon and pineapple, the retro form:** the grilled ring caramelised with 5 g brown sugar; the 1970s plate, defended on its own terms. - **Variation — the gammon hash:** dice yesterday's rested steak into the full-English hash master's potato stage — the leftover loop closed. - **The buying note:** 1.5–2 cm is the correct thickness — thin "breakfast gammon" steaks seize and dry; proper steaks sear and stay juicy. The butcher's counter, not the chiller cabinet.
